wine.name: Morgon
wine.classification: One of the ten crus of Beaujolais, above Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages
wine.sites: Old Gamay vines around Villié-Morgon, on the granite and schist of the cru, among them parcels on the Côte du Py, farmed organically and without herbicides.
wine.making: Picked by hand and carefully sorted, the grapes go into vat as whole bunches for the traditional semi carbonic maceration of the Beaujolais, ten to twenty one days on their own yeasts, with no sugar added and no sulphur in the vat. The wine is raised for about nine months in old 216 litre barrels and bottled unfiltered, some lots with a light dose of sulphur and the cuvée N with none.
wine.glass: Crushed raspberry, black cherry and violet over iron and a cool, stony note; juicy and silky, with light tannin, bright acidity and a pure, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Open and juicy within a year or two of the vintage, it keeps for about ten years, as the domaine gives it; keep a bottle without sulphur in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, lightly cool; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: One of the ten crus, around Villié-Morgon; as a cru it need not print the word Beaujolais.
The domaine's name, kept by his son and daughter after his death in 2010.

records.table: Marcel Lapierre's Morgon is the wine of the domaine at the root of natural Beaujolais: old vine Gamay fermented as whole bunches on its own yeasts, with no sugar added and little or no sulphur. Pour it lightly cool for its crushed raspberry and violet.
records.story: The Lapierre family's estate at Villié-Morgon dates, by its own account, from 1909, and Marcel Lapierre (1950 to 2010), born in the village, took it over from his father in 1973. In 1981, under the guidance of Jules Chauvet (1907 to 1989), a négociant and chemist of the Beaujolais whose research on yeasts and fermentation argued that sound grapes, carefully handled, needed little added, he changed course: he farmed organically, picked by hand and sorted hard, put whole bunches into vat, left the fermentation to the native yeasts, stopped adding sugar and used little or no sulphur. Neighbouring growers in Morgon worked the same way, and in America, where their importer gave them the name, the four became known as the Gang of Four, a nickname rather than a society. His Morgon found drinkers far beyond the Beaujolais, and the natural wine movement took it as a model. He died in October 2010, just after the harvest, and his son and daughter carried the domaine on as he had made it, bottling the Morgon in some years both with and without sulphur. The movement's argument fits in this one bottle: nothing added, and everything decided in the vineyard.

wine.name: Morgon Côte du Py
wine.classification: One of the ten crus of Beaujolais, above Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages
wine.grapes: Gamay, from old vines on the hill.
wine.sites: The Côte du Py, the hill at the heart of Morgon: old schist rich in iron oxide and manganese, weathered to the crumbly roche pourrie, rotten rock, of the growers, where the domaine's old vines grow.
wine.making: Whole bunches go into vat for a long, cool semi carbonic maceration of some three to four weeks on their own yeasts, with no sugar added and little or no sulphur; the wine is then raised for six to nine months in old barrels that once held Burgundy before bottling.
wine.glass: Dark cherry, blackberry and violet over wet slate, iron and a hint of kirsch; deeper and more savoury than most Gamay, with fine, firm tannin and a long, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Generous young, it keeps for ten years and more in a good vintage, taking on the kirsch and savour of aged Morgon.
wine.serve: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The hill of decomposed schist at the heart of Morgon, printed as a climat after the cru's name.
The cru around Villié-Morgon, with Moulin-à-Vent the one most often kept for years.

records.table: Old vines on Morgon's hill of rotten schist give Jean Foillard's Côte du Py its depth: whole bunches fermented cool with almost no sulphur, then raised in old Burgundy barrels. Darker and firmer than most Gamay, it rewards a decade in the cellar.
records.story: Morgon's growers have an old verb for what their wine does with age: it morgonne, taking on a kirsch and a savour that set it apart from the lighter crus. At the heart of the cru rises the Côte du Py, a hill of old schist rich in manganese, weathered to a crumbly rock whose wines are slow to open, and Morgon became an appellation of its own by the decree of 11 September 1936. The grower whose name the domaine carries took over his father's vines at Villié-Morgon with his wife in 1980, by most accounts. Close to Marcel Lapierre (1950 to 2010) and to the teaching of the chemist Jules Chauvet (1907 to 1989), he farmed organically, gave up cultured yeast and added sugar, kept sulphur to a minimum and let whole bunches ferment slowly in the cool. In America, where their importer gave them the name, the four Morgon growers who worked this way became known as the Gang of Four. Foillard's Côte du Py, raised in old barrels that once held Burgundy, became for many drinkers the bottle that showed how deep and long lived Gamay made with little added could be. Open a ten year old bottle for the guest who says Beaujolais never ages: the hill, as much as the cellar, is what makes it last.

wine.name: Côte de Brouilly Les Sept Vignes
wine.classification: One of the ten crus of Beaujolais, above Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages
wine.grapes: Mostly Gamay, with a small share of Chardonnay for lightness, by the estate's own account.
wine.sites: Seven parcels on the east, south and west faces of Mont Brouilly, among them Clos Bertrand, La Chapelle and Godefroy, on the hard blue stone the growers call pierre bleue: stonier high on the hill, more clayey near its foot.
wine.making: Each of the seven parcels is fermented apart in the estate's hillside cellars, partly as whole bunches in the semi carbonic way, the fermentation finishing in large oak foudres; the wine is then raised in foudre for some seven months, and the parcels are blended in the spring.
wine.glass: Cherry, raspberry and violet over crushed stone and a peppery note; firm, fine tannin, bright acidity and a saline, slightly bitter finish.
wine.ageing: Open it from its second year, as the estate advises; it keeps and gains depth for five to ten years.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, cool for a red; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The cru of the slopes of Mont Brouilly itself, a different cru from Brouilly around its foot.
The seven vineyards: the estate's parcels around the hill, fermented apart and blended into this one wine.

records.table: Château Thivin blends seven parcels from the slopes of Mont Brouilly into its Côte de Brouilly Les Sept Vignes, mostly Gamay with a touch of Chardonnay, raised in large old casks. Pour it cool for its cherry, violet and crushed stone, with charcuterie or roast chicken.
records.story: Mont Brouilly stands on its own at the southern end of the crus, a hill of hard blue stone among the granite. Shaken by the vine plagues of the nineteenth century, the growers raised a chapel on its summit in 1857, Notre-Dame du Raisin, to ask protection from the oidium that was ruining their vines. Twenty years later, on 8 June 1877, a grower from the nearby hamlet of Durette and his wife bought Château Thivin at a public sale, with a small holding of vines on the flank of the hill, and the Geoffray family's story on the hill begins there. The family worked vines on several faces of the hill, each ripening at its own pace. The growers of the slopes formed their own association in 1934, and the decree of 19 October 1938 gave them an appellation of their own, Côte de Brouilly, apart from the larger Brouilly that rings the foot of the hill. Thivin, fermenting parcel by parcel in its hillside cellars, showed what the hill gives Gamay: a firmer frame and a saline bite. Where Brouilly and Côte de Brouilly are confused, Thivin settles it: the hill and the ring around it taste different, and this is the hill.

wine.name: Moulin-à-Vent Clos de Rochegrès
wine.classification: One of the ten crus of Beaujolais, above Beaujolais and Beaujolais-Villages
wine.grapes: Gamay, the black grape with white juice.
wine.sites: Clos de Rochegrès, at some 360 metres the highest ground of Moulin-à-Vent by the estate's account, a steep slope facing south east, on shallow pink granite run through with quartz, a little more clayey than the estate's other clos.
wine.making: Picked and sorted by hand, the grapes are usually destemmed and left to macerate slowly for three to four weeks, as red Burgundy is made, rather than by carbonic maceration; the wine is then raised for about ten months in oak barrels, old and new, in the estate's old cellar.
wine.glass: Black cherry and plum over violet, liquorice and a stony, peppery note; dense and structured for Gamay, with firm, fine tannin, turning with age to dried cherry and leather.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed in youth, it is built for a decade and more, and with age its Gamay can recall a red Burgundy.
wine.serve: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour when young; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: A cru named for the windmill on its hill, not for a village; the word Beaujolais need not appear.

records.table: Château des Jacques treats its Moulin-à-Vent Clos de Rochegrès the way Burgundy treats Pinot Noir: destemmed, macerated for weeks and raised in barrel, from one clos high on the granite of the cru. Dark and firm for Gamay, give it years in the cellar.
records.story: On 31 July 1395 Philip the Bold (1342 to 1404), Duke of Burgundy, ordered Gamay torn out of the Côte d'Or as a very bad and disloyal plant, and the grape held its ground further south, on the granite hills of the Beaujolais, beyond his lands. Moulin-à-Vent takes its name from the old windmill above Romanèche-Thorins, not from any village, and it became an appellation by the decree of 11 September 1936, its vines in Romanèche-Thorins and Chénas. Château des Jacques, an estate at Romanèche-Thorins with vines in several clos of the cru, belonged to the Thorin family until 1996, when it was bought by Maison Louis Jadot, the Beaune house founded in 1859. Under Jadot the estate replanted part of its vineyard, added vines in Morgon in 2001 and renovated its winery in 2017. It destems its grapes and ages its wines in barrel, as a domaine of the Côte d'Or would, and bottles its clos apart, Clos de Rochegrès, Clos du Grand Carquelin, Champ de Cour and La Roche among them. Rochegrès, from the highest ground of the cru, shows that one clos of Gamay can carry its own name and age like Burgundy, bringing the Burgundian idea of the climat back to the grape Burgundy once banished.

wine.name: Beaujolais Nouveau
wine.grapes: Gamay, the black grape with white juice.
wine.sites: Fruit and wine bought from a great many growers and cooperatives across the region's Beaujolais appellation, rather than from vines of the house's own.
wine.making: Whole bunches go into closed vats, where the carbon dioxide of the first fermentation blankets them and many berries begin to ferment inside their skins, the semi carbonic way of the region. After a few days they are pressed, the juice finishes fermenting off the skins in steel, and the wine is bottled within weeks for release on the third Thursday of November.
wine.glass: Banana, bubblegum and kirsch over crushed raspberry and red cherry, with a touch of violet; light, juicy and soft, with almost no tannin and bright acidity.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk in its first months, by the spring after the vintage; it gains nothing in bottle.
wine.serve: 12 to 13 degrees Celsius, cool for a red; no need to decant; a plain red wine glass.

label.means: Wine of the year's harvest, released on the third Thursday of November and made to drink young.
The regional appellation; Nouveau may also be Beaujolais-Villages, but never one of the ten crus.
The négociant house of Romanèche-Thorins that buys, blends and bottles the wine.

records.table: Picked only weeks before and fermented as whole bunches under carbon dioxide, Georges Duboeuf's Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November. Banana, bubblegum and red cherry, light and juicy, it is a toast to the new harvest, so pour it cool and soon.
records.story: In 1951 the growers' union of the Beaujolais asked to sell its new wine before the general release of 15 December, and a note of the tax authorities of 13 November that year allowed it: Beaujolais Nouveau went on sale from 15 November. Georges Duboeuf (1933 to 2020), born to a family of growers in the Mâconnais, began at eighteen, as the story goes, by delivering wine by bicycle to the restaurants and chefs of the region, Lyon among them. In 1964 he set up his own business at Romanèche-Thorins, buying wine from growers across the region and bottling it under his own name, and from the 1970s, by his own account, he dressed his crus in flower labels. He made the November release an event, and by the house's account the new wine reached North America, Australia and Japan in the 1980s, where he went each year to open the first bottles. In 1985 the release was fixed on the third Thursday of November. The fashion carried the name Beaujolais round the world. He died at his home in Romanèche-Thorins in January 2020. For a sommelier the bottle is a date on the calendar and a lesson in carbonic maceration.

cards.front: Georges Duboeuf's Beaujolais Nouveau: how is it fermented?
cards.back: Whole bunches under carbon dioxide, many berries fermenting inside their skins, then pressed after a few days.

cards.front: On what day is Beaujolais Nouveau released, and since when?
cards.back: The third Thursday of November, a date fixed in 1985.

questions.q: A guest smells banana and bubblegum in a glass of Duboeuf's Beaujolais Nouveau and asks why. What do you say?
opts: Whole bunch fermentation under carbon dioxide
A banana liqueur added before bottling
Long ageing in new oak barrels
A share of Muscat in the blend
questions.exp: Carbonic maceration, whole bunches fermenting inside their skins under carbon dioxide, gives Nouveau its banana and bubblegum notes; nothing is added and the wine is raised in steel, not oak.

questions.q: Georges Duboeuf founded his négociant house at Romanèche-Thorins in 1964. In which year was the third Thursday of November fixed for Nouveau?
questions.exp: The release day was fixed on the third Thursday of November in 1985; 1951 is the year the early sale of new wine was first allowed, and 1936 the year Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent became appellations.

report: Rechecked with six searches on 12 November 2026, two of them on the house's own pages through search summaries; every source is listed in reviews/recheck-beaujolais.json.

Confirmed: Georges Duboeuf's years, 14 April 1933 to 4 January 2020, by Decanter and Wikipedia, the house of 1964, the note of 13 November 1951 with first sale on 15 November and the third Thursday fixed in 1985 by Inter Beaujolais and the INAO, and the Beaujolais-Villages Nouveau and the flower label crus by the house.

Changed: the making is the semi carbonic method of the house's Beaujolais sheets, a few days and then pressing and steel, where it said vats filled with carbon dioxide; the bicycle story has him at eighteen and is told as a story; the flower labels date from the 1970s by his account; the release abroad follows the house's account of the 1980s.

Taken out: the bistros of Lyon before 1951, the race to pour on one day in four named cities, a reputation the crus worked for decades to live down, Villages Nouveau as firmer, and the clay and limestone of the south as the source of the fruit.
No technical sheet of the house's Nouveau was found; its making is told from the house's Beaujolais sheets and the method of the region.
His birthplace is Crêches-sur-Saône in Wikipedia and Chaintré in other accounts; the record says the Mâconnais. His son, who ran the house from 2018, is living and is not named.
The pick of a Nouveau as the flagship is kept: the house is known for it worldwide, and its flower label crus stand in others.
